name: Oat extract

lead: Oat extract in skincare is mostly colloidal oatmeal or avenanthramide-standardized extract, used to calm dry, irritated skin so it looks smoother and more comfortable. It appears in sensitive-skin, baby and sun-care products.

Avenanthramides are proposed to reduce inflammation, including through NF-kappaB inhibition, and ease itch. Wikipedia states the FDA approved colloidal oatmeal as a skin protectant in 2003, and oat baths were used for itchy skin in the 19th century. Trials found for other oat extracts are mostly dietary.

paras: Used as creams, lotions, cleansers and bath soaks, often daily on dry or sensitive areas as part of a barrier-care routine.
No safety data on cosmetic oat extract were available in the sources reviewed.

news.title: Homemade Oatmeal Soap for Babies with Chamomile – Mother Earth News

angle.text: Colloidal oat and oat extracts calm dry, irritated skin through avenanthramides, so skin looks smoother and less reactive. Colloidal oatmeal holds FDA skin-protectant status.

lead: Oat extract in skincare usually means colloidal oatmeal, finely ground oat that disperses in water, or oat kernel extracts standardized for avenanthramides, phenolic compounds from Avena sativa [1][2]. It is used in cleansers, moisturizers, bath products, baby products and sun-care formulas to calm dry, itchy, easily irritated skin, which helps the skin look and feel smoother and less red. People with sensitive or reactive skin often choose oat-based products as a gentle base in a routine.

The US FDA recognizes colloidal oatmeal as a skin protectant, an approval dated to 2003 [1][2]. Oat baths for itchy skin have a long history, with references reaching back to antiquity [2]. Avenanthramides were characterized in the 1980s and are proposed as the main soothing constituents [2].

The name is also applied to unrelated preparations: oat beta-glucan fiber extracts and green-oat extracts studied as foods and supplements for cholesterol, glucose and cognition [3][4][5][6]. Skin research includes an open-label crossover trial of an oat-extract emollient for chronic itch in older adults and a laboratory study of oat extract in skin cells [7][8].
infobox: Colloidal oatmeal, kernel extract, emollient bases
Bath treatments, cleansers, moisturizers, baby and sun-care products

paras: Oat-based products are used to relieve dryness, flaking and irritation that make skin look rough or red. Oat kernel extracts with standardized avenanthramide levels appear in skin, hair, baby and sun-care products [2]. In looksmaxxing routines they typically play a supporting role as a soothing step for skin that is irritated by retinoids, acids or shaving.
Colloidal oatmeal is also sold as bath powder for widespread itchy skin.

As a recognized skin protectant, colloidal oatmeal is used for minor irritation and itching from dry skin conditions [1]. A trial in older adults with dry skin and chronic itch tested an oat-extract-based emollient [7].

Avenanthramides are phenolic alkaloids, amides formed from anthranilic acid or a derivative and a phenylpropanoid acid such as p-coumaric, ferulic or caffeic acid. Congeners A, B and C are the most abundant in oat kernels [2]. Avenanthramide C is less heat-stable than A under laboratory conditions [2].
Oats also contain beta-glucan, a soluble fiber, plus lipids and starches that give colloidal oatmeal its thickening, film-forming and moisturizing properties.

Researchers propose that avenanthramides reduce inflammation by inhibiting activation of NF-kappaB and lowering cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1; further proposals include reduced neurogenic inflammation and antihistamine-like activity [2]. A 2008 study (Sur and colleagues) is cited as reporting itch relief comparable to hydrocortisone, though Wikipedia attributes this to secondary sources [2].
A 2021 laboratory study in human keratinocytes examined an Avena sativa extract against oxidative-stress-induced apoptosis, a cell-culture model rather than a skin-appearance trial [8].

Chronic itch in older adults. A randomized, single-centre, open-label crossover study enrolled 30 adults aged 60 or older with xerosis and chronic pruritus. Participants used a Rhealba oat-extract emollient once or twice daily for two weeks and spent two weeks without treatment. Subject-rated itch on a visual analogue scale improved significantly more during treatment than during the untreated phase (P<0.0001), and investigators also assessed dry-skin score, hydration, desquamation and transepidermal water loss [7].

Dietary oat extracts. Human trials of oat extracts are mostly about food-type uses: oat fiber extracts with different beta-glucan levels and blood lipids [3], soluble oat extracts and glucose and insulin responses in moderately hypercholesterolemic adults [9], and wild green-oat extract and cognitive function in middle-aged adults, older adults and during a laboratory stressor [4][5][10][11]. A systematic review has gathered the randomized trials of Avena sativa and cognition [6].
These dietary studies do not concern skin appearance; no randomized trial of oat extract measuring wrinkles, tone or acne was found.

Oat baths are described as a long-standing folk treatment for itchy skin, sleep and anxiety, with accounts traced to ancient Egypt and Roman-era writers [2]. The FDA skin-protectant recognition in 2003 brought colloidal oatmeal into mainstream dermatology and consumer products [1][2]. A 1999 Tufts study reported that avenanthramides are bioavailable in humans, and later work reported effects of oat avenanthramide intake over eight weeks [2].

Home recipes for oatmeal soap and baths circulate in lifestyle media, for example a Mother Earth News piece on oatmeal soap for babies [12]. In looksmaxxing forums, T Nation threads mention oats as food (oatmeal recipes and breakfasts) rather than as a skin ingredient [13].

Oat is a food, and oat products are widely used on babies and sensitive skin. The Wikipedia article on avenanthramides does not discuss adverse effects [2]. Product labels typically carry patch-test and discontinue-if-irritated guidance as for other cosmetics.

lore.intro: Oat extract is rarely a topic on looksmaxxing forums as a skin ingredient; the T Nation material in this area concerns oatmeal as food [13]. The claims below are the common ones in skincare discussion.

claims.claim: Oat extract soothes itchy, irritated skin
Avenanthramides work like a mild steroid for itch
Oat extract improves wrinkles or skin tone

timeline.event: Avenanthramides first isolated and characterized by Collins [2].
Collins synthesizes several avenanthramides and confirms they match the natural compounds [2].
A Tufts study reports avenanthramides are bioavailable and active in humans [2].
Colloidal oatmeal approved by the US FDA as a skin protectant, per Wikipedia [1][2].
Randomized crossover trial of an oat-extract emollient for chronic itch in older adults [7].
